arml-local-2009-team-01.title: Use the conjugate root
arml-local-2009-team-01.body:
Since $A,B$ are real, the other root is the conjugate $3-2i$. Then $-A$ is the sum of the roots, $6$, and $B$ is their product, $(3+2i)(3-2i)=9+4=13$.

**Answer: $(A,B)=(-6,13)$**

arml-local-2009-team-01.title: Substitute directly
arml-local-2009-team-01.body:
$(3+2i)^2+A(3+2i)+B=(9-4+12i)+3A+2Ai+B=(5+3A+B)+(12+2A)i=0$. The imaginary part gives $A=-6$, then the real part gives $5-18+B=0$, so $B=13$.

**Answer: $(A,B)=(-6,13)$**

arml-local-2009-team-02.title: Compose linear functions
arml-local-2009-team-02.body:
Write $f(x)=-3x+b$. Composing lines multiplies slopes, so $f(f(x))$ has slope $(-3)^2=9$ and $f(f(f(x)))$ has slope $(-3)^3=-27$. The slope of the sum is the sum of the slopes: $-27+9-3=-21$.

**Answer: $-21$**

arml-local-2009-team-03.title: Expected money per roll times expected number of rolls
arml-local-2009-team-03.body:
Each roll is worth $\frac{12+16+26}{3}=18$ dollars on average, and the number of rolls $N$ is a stopping time, so the expected winnings equal $18\cdot E[N]$.

- $N=2$ when the second roll repeats the first amount: probability $\frac13$.
- $N=3$ when the second roll is new ($\frac23$) and the third repeats one of the two seen amounts ($\frac23$): probability $\frac49$.
- $N=4$ otherwise (a fourth roll must repeat): probability $1-\frac13-\frac49=\frac29$.

$E[N]=2\cdot\frac13+3\cdot\frac49+4\cdot\frac29=\frac{26}{9}$, so the expected winnings are $\frac{26}{9}\cdot18=52$.

**Answer: 52 dollars**

arml-local-2009-team-03.title: Add up each case directly
arml-local-2009-team-03.body:
- Ends after 2 rolls (prob. $\frac13$): the winnings are $2v$ where $v$ is the repeated amount, average $2\cdot18=36$. Contribution $\frac13\cdot36=12$.
- Ends after 3 rolls (prob. $\frac49$): two different amounts $x,y$ (average total $36$) plus a repeat of one of them (average $18$): $54$. Contribution $\frac49\cdot54=24$.
- Ends after 4 rolls (prob. $\frac29$): all three amounts ($12+16+26=54$) plus a repeat (average $18$): $72$. Contribution $\frac29\cdot72=16$.

Total $12+24+16=52$.

**Answer: 52 dollars**

arml-local-2009-team-04.title: Split the power
arml-local-2009-team-04.body:
$3^{f(3)+f(9)}=3^{\log_3 5}\cdot 3^{\log_9 11}$. The first factor is $5$. For the second, $3=9^{1/2}$, so $3^{\log_9 11}=\left(9^{\log_9 11}\right)^{1/2}=\sqrt{11}$.

**Answer: $5\sqrt{11}$**

arml-local-2009-team-05.title: Complete to an equilateral triangle
arml-local-2009-team-05.body:
Every angle of the hexagon is $120^\circ$. Extend $AB$, $CD$, $EF$ until they meet in a triangle $XYZ$; its angles are all $60^\circ$, so it is equilateral, and cutting off the hexagon leaves three small equilateral triangles with sides $BC=3$, $DE=u$ and $FA=v$ (next to $B,C$; $D,E$; $F,A$).

The three sides of $XYZ$ are $v+3+3$, $3+8+u$ and $u+5+v$. Setting them equal: $6+v=u+5+v$ gives $u=1$, and then $6+v=12$ gives $v=6$. The side of $XYZ$ is $12$.

Area $=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\left(12^2-6^2-3^2-1^2\right)=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\cdot98=\frac{49\sqrt3}{2}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{49\sqrt3}{2}$**

arml-local-2009-team-06.title: Square both sides
arml-local-2009-team-06.body:
Squaring gives $1+2|\sin\theta\cos\theta|=\frac{16}{9}$, i.e. $|\sin2\theta|=\frac79$. As $\theta$ runs over $[0,2\pi]$, $2\theta$ runs over $[0,4\pi]$, two full periods. In each period $\sin\phi=\frac79$ has 2 solutions and $\sin\phi=-\frac79$ has 2 solutions, giving $8$ solutions in all. (Squaring is reversible since both sides are positive.)

**Answer: 8**

arml-local-2009-team-06.title: Geometric picture
arml-local-2009-team-06.body:
The points $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ lie on the unit circle, and $|x|+|y|=\frac43$ is a square with vertices $(\pm\frac43,0),(0,\pm\frac43)$. Since $1<\frac43<\sqrt2$ the square's sides cut the unit circle, each side in two points, so there are $4\cdot2=8$ intersections.

**Answer: 8**

arml-local-2009-team-07.title: Count the arrangements
arml-local-2009-team-07.body:
There are $\binom{9}{4}=126$ equally likely arrangements. In a box you win if it holds 0 red balls, tie if 1, and lose if $\ge2$.

If every box holds at most 2 red balls, the possible patterns are $(2,2,1,0,0)$, $(2,1,1,1,0)$, $(1,1,1,1,1)$, and in each of them you win and lose the same number of boxes (2 and 2, 1 and 1, 0 and 0), so you do not win. If some box has $\ge3$ red balls, the other red balls can beat at most one more box, so you win more boxes than the opponent. E.g. $(3,1,1,0,0)$: you win 2, lose 1; $(3,2,0,0,0)$: you win 3, lose 2.

The number of arrangements with all counts $\le2$: $\frac{5!}{2!\,1!\,2!}+\frac{5!}{1!\,3!\,1!}+1=30+20+1=51$. So you win in $126-51=75$ arrangements, probability $\frac{75}{126}=\frac{25}{42}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{25}{42}$**

arml-local-2009-team-08.title: Legendre's formula and base 5
arml-local-2009-team-08.body:
The term $x^ay^bz^c$ ($a+b+c=2009$) has coefficient $\frac{2009!}{a!\,b!\,c!}$. Using $v_5(m!)=\frac{m-s_5(m)}{4}$ ($s_5$ = digit sum in base 5),
$$v_5\!\left(\tfrac{2009!}{a!b!c!}\right)=\frac{s_5(a)+s_5(b)+s_5(c)-s_5(2009)}{4}.$$
This is $0$ exactly when adding $a+b+c$ in base 5 involves no carries, i.e. in every base-5 position the digits of $a,b,c$ add up to the digit of $2009$.

$2009=3\cdot625+1\cdot125+0\cdot25+1\cdot5+4=(31014)_5$. A digit $d$ can be split into three non-negative digits in $\binom{d+2}{2}$ ways, so
$$k=\binom52\binom32\binom22\binom32\binom62=10\cdot3\cdot1\cdot3\cdot15=1350.$$

**Answer: 1350**

arml-local-2009-team-09.title: Coordinates
arml-local-2009-team-09.body:
Put $A=(0,0)$, $B=(3,0)$, $C=\left(\frac32,\frac{3\sqrt3}2\right)$. Then $D=\left(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)$ (a third of the way along $AC$) and, by symmetry, $E=\left(\frac52,\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)$.

Line $AE$: $(\frac52t,\frac{\sqrt3}2t)$. Line $BD$: $(3-\frac52s,\frac{\sqrt3}2s)$. Equal heights force $s=t$, then $\frac52t=3-\frac52t$ gives $t=\frac35$, so $F=\left(\frac32,\frac{3\sqrt3}{10}\right)$.

Area of $ADF$ with $A$ at the origin: $\frac12\left|x_Dy_F-x_Fy_D\right|=\frac12\left|\frac12\cdot\frac{3\sqrt3}{10}-\frac32\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right|=\frac12\cdot\frac{6\sqrt3}{10}=\frac{3\sqrt3}{10}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{3\sqrt3}{10}$**

arml-local-2009-team-09.title: Area ratios
arml-local-2009-team-09.body:
Triangle $ABD$ has area $\frac{AD}{AC}[ABC]=\frac13\cdot\frac{9\sqrt3}{4}=\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}$. Apply Menelaus to triangle $BCD$ with the line through $A$, $F$, $E$: $\frac{CA}{AD}\cdot\frac{DF}{FB}\cdot\frac{BE}{EC}=1$, so $3\cdot\frac{DF}{FB}\cdot\frac12=1$ and $\frac{DF}{FB}=\frac23$, i.e. $DF=\frac25DB$. Triangles $ADF$ and $ABD$ have the same height from $A$, so $[ADF]=\frac25\cdot\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}=\frac{3\sqrt3}{10}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{3\sqrt3}{10}$**
